questions.stem: According to Ohm's Law, if a potential difference of V is applied across a conductor carrying current I, the electrical resistance R is:
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law: V = IR, so R = V/I. Resistance is measured in Ohms (Ω). Ohm's Law holds for ohmic conductors (metals at constant temperature) but not for non-ohmic devices like diodes or filament bulbs.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: When resistors are connected in parallel, which electrical quantity remains the same across all resistors?
questions.explanation: In a parallel circuit, all resistors share the same two end nodes, so the voltage (potential difference) across each is identical. The current distributes — higher current flows through lower resistance. Home electrical circuits are parallel so each appliance gets the same supply voltage.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The SI unit of electric power is:
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of energy transfer. The SI unit of power is the Watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. For AC circuits, real power is in Watts; apparent power is in Volt-Amperes (VA). The Joule is the unit of energy, and Coulomb is the unit of charge.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Faraday's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction were discovered in which year?
questions.explanation: Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831 — demonstrating that a changing magnetic flux induces an EMF in a conductor. His First Law: an EMF is induced whenever magnetic flux through a circuit changes. His Second Law: the induced EMF = rate of change of magnetic flux.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule is used to determine the direction of which quantity in an electric motor?
options: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (motor principle)
Induced EMF in a generator or dynamo
Magnetic field around a solenoid carrying current
Direction of conventional current flow in a circuit
questions.explanation: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule (for motors): stretch thumb, index finger, and middle finger mutually perpendicular. Index → field direction (B), Middle → current direction (I), Thumb → thrust/force direction (F). It applies to electric motors that convert electrical energy to mechanical energy.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: In a step-up transformer, which of the following correctly describes the relationship between primary and secondary voltages?
options: Secondary voltage is less than primary voltage
Secondary voltage is greater than primary voltage (turns ratio N₂ > N₁)
Primary and secondary voltages are equal
Secondary current is always greater than primary current
questions.explanation: In a step-up transformer: N₂ > N₁ (more turns in secondary), so V₂ > V₁. By conservation of energy (ideal transformer): V₁I₁ = V₂I₂, so if voltage increases, current decreases proportionally. Step-up transformers are used at power stations to raise voltage for long-distance transmission.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The standard AC mains electricity supply frequency in India is:
questions.explanation: India uses 50 Hz AC at 230 V (single phase). The USA and Canada use 60 Hz. Frequency determines how many times per second the current direction reverses (50 times in India). Higher frequency reduces transformer core losses but increases cable charging current losses.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh), the commercial unit of electrical energy ('1 unit' on electricity bills), is equal to:
questions.explanation: 1 kWh = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3.6 MJ. This is the energy consumed by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour. One 'unit' of electricity on domestic bills = 1 kWh. Short Trick: kWh to Joules → multiply by 3.6 × 10⁶.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Lenz's Law states that the direction of the induced current in a conductor is always such that it:
options: Opposes the change in magnetic flux that caused the induction
Increases the rate of change of magnetic flux to maintain current
Flows in the same direction as the inducing primary current
Is independent of the inducing magnetic field direction
questions.explanation: Lenz's Law (a consequence of energy conservation): the induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux causing it. If a north pole approaches a coil, the induced current creates a north pole (repelling it) — opposing the increase in flux. This is how braking in regenerative braking systems works.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Resistors R₁ = 2 Ω, R₂ = 3 Ω, and R₃ = 5 Ω are connected in series to a 10 V battery. The total current flowing through the circuit is:
questions.explanation: Series circuit: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω. By Ohm's Law: I = V/R = 10 V / 10 Ω = 1 A. Short Trick: In series, same current flows through all — add resistances, then divide voltage by total R.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The geographic North Pole of the Earth is located near the:
options: Magnetically neutral zone at the geographic pole
South magnetic pole (geomagnetic south) of the Earth's internal field
questions.explanation: Earth's geographic North Pole is a magnetic south pole — a compass needle (which is a bar magnet) points toward geographic North because that region is a magnetic south (opposite poles attract). The Earth's magnetic field emerges from near the geographic South Pole (geomagnetic north) and enters at the geographic North Pole (geomagnetic south).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. Their equivalent resistance is:
questions.explanation: 1/R_eq = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. Therefore R_eq = 2 Ω. Short Trick: For two resistors in parallel, R_eq = (R₁ × R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. Parallel equivalent is always less than the smallest resistor.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Fleming's Right-Hand Rule is used to determine the direction of:
options: Induced EMF (or current) in a generator/dynamo when a conductor moves in a magnetic field
Force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field
Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet
Electric field inside a parallel-plate capacitor
questions.explanation: Fleming's Right-Hand Rule (for generators): stretch thumb, index, and middle fingers mutually perpendicular. Thumb → motion direction of conductor, Index → magnetic field direction, Middle → induced current direction. It applies to dynamos (mechanical → electrical energy).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A 100 W electric bulb is kept on for 5 hours. The electrical energy consumed in kilowatt-hours (kWh) is:
questions.explanation: Energy = Power × Time = 100 W × 5 h = 500 Wh = 0.5 kWh. Short Trick: Energy (kWh) = Power (kW) × Time (h) = 0.1 kW × 5 h = 0.5 kWh. This would cost 0.5 units on an electricity bill.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A solenoid (a tightly wound cylindrical coil) carrying current behaves magnetically like:
options: A bar magnet with north and south poles at its ends
questions.explanation: A current-carrying solenoid has a uniform magnetic field inside and field lines outside that are identical to a bar magnet (dipole pattern). One end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole, determined by the direction of current using the right-hand rule.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A transformer has 100 turns in the primary coil and 2,000 turns in the secondary coil. If the primary voltage is 220 V, the secondary (output) voltage is:
questions.explanation: Transformer equation: V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁. V₂ = V₁ × (N₂/N₁) = 220 × (2,000/100) = 220 × 20 = 4,400 V. This is a step-up transformer (20:1 turns ratio). Short Trick: turns ratio = voltage ratio for an ideal transformer.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The phenomenon by which certain materials lose all electrical resistance below a critical temperature (called the critical temperature Tc) is known as:
questions.explanation: Superconductivity, discovered by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911 (mercury at 4.2 K), is the zero electrical resistance state. Superconductors are used in MRI machines, particle accelerators (CERN), and maglev trains. High-temperature superconductors (YBCO, Tc ~93 K) are an active research area.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The power dissipated in a resistor R when a current I flows through it is given by:
questions.explanation: Power P = I²R (derived from P = VI and V = IR: P = I × IR = I²R). Alternatively, P = V²/R. Short Trick: Power formulae — P = VI = I²R = V²/R. For a constant voltage supply, P ∝ 1/R; for constant current, P ∝ R.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: An electric motor converts energy from one form to another. It converts:
questions.explanation: An electric motor converts electrical energy → mechanical (kinetic) energy, using the principle that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (Lorentz force). A generator (dynamo) does the reverse — mechanical → electrical.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The SI unit of electric charge is:
questions.explanation: The SI unit of electric charge is the Coulomb (C). 1 Coulomb = charge carried by a current of 1 Ampere flowing for 1 second (Q = It). An electron carries a charge of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The Ampere is the unit of current, Volt of potential difference, and Ohm of resistance.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A generator (dynamo) works on the principle of:
options: Ohm's Law relating V, I, and R
Ampere's circuital law for magnetic field due to current
Coulomb's Law for force between charges
questions.explanation: A generator works on Faraday's Law — a rotating coil in a magnetic field experiences changing magnetic flux, which induces an EMF (and hence current in a closed circuit). AC generators produce alternating current; DC generators use a commutator to produce direct current.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The resistivity of a metallic conductor with increasing temperature:
options: Decreases, because atoms vibrate less at higher temperatures
Increases, because more frequent collisions between electrons and atoms impede current flow
Decreases for all materials at higher temperatures
questions.explanation: For metals, resistivity increases with temperature (positive temperature coefficient). At higher temperatures, lattice ions vibrate more vigorously, causing more electron-ion collisions and greater resistance to current flow. Exception: semiconductors (Si, Ge) have negative temperature coefficient — their resistivity decreases with rising temperature.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: In high-voltage AC transmission lines, very high voltages are used to transmit power over long distances primarily because:
options: High voltage reduces transmission current (I = P/V), minimizing power loss (P_loss = I²R) in cables
High voltage increases current flow to speed up delivery
High voltage is safer for substation transformers to handle
High voltage eliminates the need for step-down transformers at the receiving end
questions.explanation: Transmission power P = VI. For the same power, higher V means lower I. Power lost in transmission line resistance R: P_loss = I²R. So reducing I dramatically reduces loss (squared relationship). Short Trick: Doubling V halves I, reducing power loss by 4×. India transmits at 220 kV, 400 kV, 765 kV, and now 1,200 kV (UHVAC).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. The power dissipated in the resistor is:
questions.explanation: P = V²/R = (12)²/4 = 144/4 = 36 W. Alternatively: I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A; P = I²R = 9 × 4 = 36 W. Short Trick: P = V²/R is fastest when voltage is given directly.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Electromagnets are widely used in electric bells and relays because, unlike permanent magnets, they:
options: Provide a stronger and more permanent magnetic force
Are naturally magnetic without any power supply
Can be magnetized and demagnetized rapidly simply by switching the electric current on and off
Cost significantly less than permanent magnets
questions.explanation: Electromagnets generate magnetic fields only when current flows through their coils. This on-off controllability makes them ideal for electric bells (striker moves when energized), relays (switching heavy currents), cranes (lifting and releasing scrap metal), and MRI machines (tunable field strength).
questions.subject: Physics
